nagoya_niku_udon_sansuke.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner Katō spent years training in ramen rather than udon — he worked at the legendary Ramen Jiro Mita main branch, then ran the Ramen Jiro Ōmiya offshoot for eight years before pivoting to udon in Nagoya. He opened this counter in October 2017 at age 29, channeling his ramen ped

chef_bio.background: Owner Katō Shōgo built his craft in ramen rather than udon. After about a year in an izakaya kitchen and roughly five years of ramen training — including time at the legendary Ramen Jirō Mita main branch — he opened his own Ramen Jirō Ōmiya shop in Saitama at age 29 and ran it for eight years, before pivoting to udon in Nagoya. He opened this Marunouchi counter on 17 October 2017, channeling his ramen pedigree into a bowl that straddles both worlds.
chef_bio.philosophy: Always satisfy the customer's appetite (必ずお腹を満足させる). Katō applies ramen-kitchen discipline — notably a three-day-marinated house chashu — to an udon format, producing generous portions that reviewers describe as addictive despite their richness.
chef_bio.specialty: さんすけうどん — handmade thick flat noodles in a rich, tamari-soy-forward broth (the tamari sourced from a Gifu maker) topped with house chashu and sweet-savory braised pork; the bowl reads so much like Yokohama iekei ramen that noodle-hunters do a double-take.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name, さんすけ, references Oda Nobunaga's childhood name (三介) — a playful local anchor for what is otherwise a very non-traditional udon.
A food blogger visiting in summer 2025 noted customers eating with smiles and laughter — a warm contrast to the tense, almost martial atmosphere of the Ramen Jiro style the owner came from.
The broth prompted one writer to ask 'Is this just Yokohama ie-kei ramen?' — the tamari-soy, pork-bone, chicken-oil combination reads unmistakably ramen to veteran noodle-hunters.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official amebaownd site gives owner 加藤省吾, opening 17 Oct 2017, the motto 必ずお腹を満足させる, a first shop opened at 29 in Ōmiya run for eight years, three-day-marinated chashu, and Gifu tamari soy. The sehensucht blog confirms the Ramen Jiro Mita/Omiya pedigree, the 三介 name origin, and the iekei-like broth.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles are the restaurant's entire product; flour is present throughout the kitchen. No gluten-free alternative exists and cross-contamination is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth uses Imokei tamari soy sauce from Gifu Prefecture. Tamari is typically made with little or no wheat, but this has not been confirmed as certified gluten-free and is served in a wheat-noodle kitchen.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork chashu, chicken oil, and animal dashi are core broth components. There is no vegan path through the menu.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Staff are noted as patient and thorough in explaining the menu to first-time visitors, but no allergy or dietary accommodation protocols have been documented by any source.

cultural_comfort.note: Cash-only counter shop with a local-regular feel; staff are described as attentive and happy to explain the menu, but all signage and interaction is in Japanese.

nagoya_grazie_di_cuore.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering is listed or advertised. All pizzas and fresh pasta are wheat-based; the restaurant's own website highlights Italian wheat flour (イタリア産小麦) as a point of pride in its pizza dough. There is no dedicated GF kitchen, no mention of GF flour alternatives, and no allergen menu. Cross-contamination from flour-heavy cooking is a real concern. The restaurant does accept allergy-substitution requests verbally, but suitability for celiac diners has not been established.
nagoya_grazie_di_cuore.vegan_detail: No vegan designation. The menu is built around meat, cheese, seafood, and egg-enriched pasta (carbonara uses Nagoya Cochin egg). Organic vegetables appear throughout — salads, roasted vegetables, and sides — but no dish is explicitly vegan. The restaurant notes it accommodates ingredient-substitution requests at time of visit, so it is worth asking, but no vegan commitment is made.
nagoya_grazie_di_cuore.hours_raw: Mon–Wed, Fri–Sun 11:00–14:00 (L.O. 13:30) / 17:30–22:00 (L.O. 21:00), closed Thu (open on holidays)
nagoya_grazie_di_cuore.notes: Born in Tokyo in 1982, Terasawa Takashi discovered a love of cooking during part-time work at a family restaurant chain, where he stayed for eight years. He then spent three years at a pizza specialty shop, followed by three years at an Italian restaurant, before being entrusted

chef_bio.background: Born in Tokyo in 1982, Terasawa Takashi discovered a love of cooking during part-time work at a family-restaurant chain, where he stayed for eight years. He then spent three years at a pizza specialty shop, followed by three years at an Italian restaurant, before being entrusted with the kitchen at Grazie di Cuore.
chef_bio.philosophy: 'Joshin Italian' (浄心イタリアン) — Italian food seasoned and sourced to suit Japanese palates so that diners of every age feel at home with it (日本人が食べやすい味付けや食材にした料理は若い方から年配の方にも好評).
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-made pizza on a custom blend of Italian wheat flour rested for half a day, fired to a crisp exterior and chewy interior; house-made roast beef is another signature.

anecdotes.text: Terasawa's pizzas became so sought-after by fellow restaurateurs that the shop launched a frozen-pizza wholesale line — now supplying Italian restaurants, cafes, izakayas, and bars across the region (desserts are also popular with yakiniku shops).

The chef's route into professional cooking began entirely through family-restaurant part-time work; his eight years there gave him the fundamentals before he moved to specialist pizza and Italian training.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Suchikon-tatsujin confirms chef 寺澤昴志, born Tokyo 1982, and the 8yr/3yr/3yr training path; grazie.nagoya confirms the Joshin-ku location, Japanese-palate philosophy, and (via listings) the Italian-wheat dough rested half a day; the business page confirms the frozen-pizza wholesale line.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen works extensively with Italian wheat flour for fresh pasta and pizza dough; no GF-separated preparation area or equipment is mentioned.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No soy sauce-based dishes are evident on the Italian menu, but standard wheat-containing Italian ingredients (pasta dough, pizza dough) are used throughout.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Cheese, prosciutto, and animal-based ingredients appear in nearly every menu section; no vegan-safe prep line is indicated.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The restaurant states it accepts ingredient-substitution requests for allergies or dietary preferences at the time of visit (要相談).

positives.text: Organic vegetables (有機野菜) are used throughout the menu in salads, pasta, and side dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A neighborhood Italian with local regulars and no evident English signage or menu; basic Japanese phrases will get you far, and staff are described as friendly and welcoming.

nagoya_teuchi_soba_sougen.gf_detail: [Held at "ask" 2026-08-20] The description below was not traceable to any source, so the GF label is held down until it is. The restaurant specialises in 十割そば (juwari soba) — 100% buckwheat noodles, which contain no wheat flour. This is a genuine option for gluten-avoiders. However, the standard offering also includes 二八そば (niwari, 20% wheat) and 更科そば (sarashina, also wheat-blended), so you must explicitly request the 十割. The tsuyu is made with a 20-year-old kaeshi base using shoyu from Shinshu (Nagano) — standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Cross-contamination risk exists because wheat-containing soba is kneaded and cut in the same kitchen. No dedicated gluten-free kitchen is claimed. Tempura is served, meaning wheat flour and shared frying oil are present. Suitable for gluten-preference only, not celiac safety.
nagoya_teuchi_soba_sougen.vegan_detail: Soba noodles themselves can be ordered without animal products, but the tsuyu (dipping broth) is almost certainly based on katsuobushi (bonito) and/or conventional Japanese dashi — no vegan broth option is advertised. Signature dishes include kamo-nanban (duck broth) and pork dipping soba; tempura is on the menu. Vegans should call ahead to ask whether a plain cold soba with no dipping sauce or a substitute is possible.

chef_bio.background: Opened on 27 March 2006 on the ground floor of the Nakabun Building in Nagoya's Marunouchi office district (5 minutes from Hisaya-odori Station). The owner-operator hand-rolls every portion of soba each morning using stone-milled buckwheat ground fresh daily. The shop's kaeshi (the soy-sauce base of the tsuyu) has been continuously replenished since opening and has now reached about 20 years of age.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner selects buckwheat and adjusts the milling to coax the maximum aroma and flavour from the grain itself, offering both juwari (100% buckwheat) and delicate sarashina. The tsuyu is built on a single carefully chosen Shinshu (Nagano) shoyu that has not changed since the shop opened.
chef_bio.specialty: Juwari soba (十割そば) — 100% buckwheat noodles; also kamo-nanban (duck) dipping soba and seasonal tempura

anecdotes.text: The shop's kaeshi has been continuously replenished since the 2006 opening and now spans roughly 20 years — a hallmark of a traditional soba-ya — paired with a single Shinshu shoyu unchanged since day one.
An early food-blog review noted that 100% buckwheat soba was available as a small (¥100) upcharge over the standard nihachi, with pork and duck dipping broths as the signature warm options.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog confirms the 27 Mar 2006 opening, Nakabun Bldg location, self-milled juwari/sarashina and duck-broth soba; the official about page (indexed) confirms the unchanged Shinshu shoyu and a ~20-year kaeshi; the ameblo blog confirms the ¥100 juwari upcharge and pork/duck dipping broths.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-containing niwari (80% buckwheat / 20% wheat) and sarashina soba are made in the same kitchen as the juwari (100% buckwheat) soba; shared surfaces and equipment are likely.
gf_cross_contamination.why: NIWARI IS NOT ON THE MENU. Both the cited Tabelog page and the shop's own archived about page say the shop offers exactly two soba: 十割 and 更科; a review records staff asking 「蕎麦は十割でよろしいですか」 because juwari is the default. Neither page says the sarashina contains wheat. Rewrite the shared-kitchen claim

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsuyu is built on a 20-year-old kaeshi made with Shinshu shoyu — standard Japanese soy sauce brewed with wheat. All broth-based and dipping dishes will contain wheat-derived soy sauce.
soy_sauce_wheat.source_wording: 創愿のつゆの決め手となる醤油は、当店開業以来変わることのない店主 こだわり の醤油を使用しております。… 醤油を信州より取り寄せております。 (web.archive.org/web/20180828153042)

vegan_cross_contact.text: Tempura is on the menu, meaning wheat-batter frying takes place in the kitchen. Duck (kamo) and pork dipping broths are signature items, so animal products are central to the cooking environment.
vegan_cross_contact.why: PORK IS INVENTED. 豚 appears nowhere on the cited page or the menu page. The three signature tsukejiru are 黒鴨 / 白鴨 / 赤海老 — duck, duck and SHRIMP. Swap 'pork' for 'shrimp'; the vegan conclusion is unaffected and is strengthened by 鰹節 in the white dashi, 鴨ロース and だしまき (egg).

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergy menu, allergy statement, or staff allergy-handling protocol has been published on any source reviewed. Guests with serious allergies should call 052-951-1226 before visiting.
staff_allergy_handling.why: CONTRADICTED BY THE CITED PAGE. It says 'customers with a buckwheat allergy are asked to refrain from visiting' — that IS a published allergy statement, and a consequential one: this shop declines allergy patrons rather than accommodating them. Rewrite as 'the shop publicly asks buckwheat-allergic g

positives.text: Juwari soba (十割そば, 100% buckwheat, no wheat flour in the noodle itself) is a standing menu option and represents a genuine wheat-free noodle choice for those avoiding gluten by preference.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet, polished soba-ya in a business district with no English signage noted; an English menu is reportedly available, but interaction will be primarily in Japanese.

nagoya_teuchi_soba_futaba.gf_detail: The menu includes both 二八そば (nihachi: 80% buckwheat, 20% wheat — not gluten-free) and 十割そば (juwari: 100% buckwheat — wheat-free as a flour). However, this is a general soba kitchen with no dedicated gluten-free protocol confirmed. The dashi broth uses bonito (likely with standard soy sauce containing wheat). Tempura is also on the menu, introducing wheat batter and shared-fryer risk. Celiacs should call ahead; the juwari soba is the only potentially lower-wheat option and cross-contamination cannot be ruled out.
nagoya_teuchi_soba_futaba.vegan_detail: The dashi stock is bonito-based (katsuo dashi), making the standard soba broth non-vegan. The tsuyu served with cold seiro soba is also fish-based. Duck dishes are on the menu. Vegetable tempura options exist but share the kitchen. No plant-based broth alternative is mentioned anywhere. Vegans should ask if a konbu-only dashi is available; assume not unless confirmed.

chef_bio.philosophy: A calm, unhurried neighborhood soba shop where the noodles are rolled fresh daily and the atmosphere encourages lingering over soba-yu at the end of the meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-rolled nihachi (80/20 buckwheat-wheat) and juwari (100% buckwheat) seiro soba, cut thin with a firm bite; duck-nanban seiro and tempura seiro (shrimp and vegetable) are the standout dishes.

anecdotes.text: Despite being a small shop (about six seats), diners line up at the door by the 6 pm dinner opening — a reliable sign of neighborhood loyalty.
A soba researcher visiting in 2024 noted the mild, pale-coloured broth and hand-rolled noodles at roughly 130–140 g per serving, and left wishing they had asked about the buckwheat's origin.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Nihon-soba.jp (2024) confirms nihachi/juwari seiro, duck-nanban and tempura seiro, the mild pale broth, ~130-140g thin firm noodles, the 6pm dinner opening, six seats, and that the reviewer didn't learn the buckwheat origin; 4travel corroborates the queue at opening.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area is documented. The kitchen handles both wheat-containing nihachi noodles and tempura batter alongside the 100% buckwheat juwari soba, making cross-contamination a realistic concern for celiacs.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsuyu dipping broth and kakejiru hot broth are almost certainly made with standard soy sauce (which contains wheat) and bonito dashi — no wheat-free tamari alternative is mentioned anywhere.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bonito-based dashi is the standard broth throughout; duck dishes are prepared in the same kitchen. No plant-based alternative broth has been confirmed.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergen handling procedures or staff allergy awareness information has been published for this restaurant. Phone ahead (052-522-5660) for any dietary requirements.

positives.text: The juwari (十割) seiro uses 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat added to the noodle itself — the safest option on the menu for those avoiding wheat in the noodle strand, subject to kitchen cross-contamination caveats.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet neighborhood soba-ya with no English signage or menu noted; a few Japanese phrases for ordering or pointing at the menu is enough to get by.

nagoya_noko_chuka_soba_sato.gf_detail: The broth is built on tamari soy sauce — even tamari often contains trace wheat in Japanese commercial production. No gluten-free claims or allergen accommodations are mentioned anywhere. The noodles themselves contain wheat. No dedicated fryer information available as this is a noodle shop. Not safe for celiac diners.
nagoya_noko_chuka_soba_sato.vegan_detail: The broth is a pork bone and pork meat (豚骨・豚肉) base seasoned with tamari soy sauce. Chashu (braised pork belly) is the signature topping. No vegan or vegetarian options mentioned. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
nagoya_noko_chuka_soba_sato.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:00–14:00, 17:30–20:30 (closes once soup runs out) / Sat & holidays 11:00–14:00 / closed Sun and the 2nd Saturday
nagoya_noko_chuka_soba_sato.notes: [Mom & Pop] Opened in October 2018 in Nagoya's Marunouchi business district, Noko Chuka Soba Sato was born from a bold genre pivot: the owner had previously run a popular donburi (rice bowl) restaurant called Le Granbowl at or near the same location, building deep expertise in meat preparati

chef_bio.background: Opened in October 2018 in Nagoya's Marunouchi business district, Noko Chuka Soba Sato was born from a bold genre pivot: the same premises had housed the owner's popular donburi (rice-bowl) restaurant, Le Granbowl (れ・ぐらんぼる), where he built deep expertise in meat preparation before committing fully to ramen. It is a small (~16-seat) counter-focused shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: Despite the dramatic visual of a meat-piled bowl, the broth is treated as the centerpiece — a concentrated pork-based stock seasoned with dark tamari soy and finished with subtle garlic and sweet notes — with the toppings as supporting cast.
chef_bio.specialty: 濃厚チャーシュー中華そば — a rich tamari-soy broth loaded with roughly ten thin slices of precisely prepared pork belly arranged in a flower-like spread across the bowl, over medium-thick, slightly firm noodles.

anecdotes.text: The shop transformed from a donburi specialist (Le Granbowl) into a ramen destination, carrying over the owner's confident meat-butchery skill into the chashu preparation that now defines the bowl.
A table condiment of kombu vinegar (昆布酢) is provided to cut the richness of the broth and add umami — an unusual and praised touch that regulars use to shift the flavour mid-bowl.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Jouhou.nagoya confirms the 11 Oct 2018 opening in Marunouchi, ~16 seats, the Le Granbowl donburi predecessor, the tamari broth and decoratively piled chashu; nagoya-meshi confirms roughly ten flower-arranged pork-belly slices and the kombu-vinegar condiment.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No gluten-free accommodations exist. Wheat noodles are the core product cooked in the same kitchen, making cross-contamination certain.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Broth is seasoned with tamari soy sauce; tamari in Japanese commercial production frequently contains trace wheat, and no wheat-free tamari claim is made.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broth is pork-based; no plant-based or separate cooking line exists.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergy-handling protocols or allergen menus are mentioned on any source reviewed. Phone lines are closed during service hours.

cultural_comfort.note: Counter-style ramen shop serving a Japanese business-district crowd; no English menu or staff noted, but ordering is straightforward with a short menu.

nagoya_rakuichi.gf_detail: No gluten-free claims or accommodations found. The tare (seasoning sauce) in tonkotsu ramen is typically wheat-based soy sauce, making the broth unsafe for celiac diners. Noodles are standard wheat noodles. Gyoza and other sides contain wheat. Cross-contamination risk is high in this tiny open counter kitchen. Not suitable for gluten-free diners.
nagoya_rakuichi.vegan_detail: The broth is tonkotsu (pork bone) and the tare almost certainly contains soy sauce. Chashu pork is a standard topping. No plant-based options are listed. This shop is not suitable for vegans.
nagoya_rakuichi.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, hidden-gem counter ramen shop tucked in a quiet residential street in Nishi Ward, close to Meijo Park. Reviewers describe it as a place that feels more like a neighbourhood izakaya than a ramen shop, with regulars ordering beer and appetisers alongside bowls.

chef_bio.background: A small, hidden-gem counter ramen shop (about ten seats) tucked in a quiet part of Nishi Ward near a driving school, close to Meijo Park. The proprietor runs it solo, and reviewers describe it as feeling more like a neighbourhood izakaya than a ramen shop, with regulars ordering beer and appetisers alongside bowls.
chef_bio.philosophy: Unpretentious neighbourhood comfort — the worn exterior belies a welcoming, easy atmosphere where solo diners and locals linger.
chef_bio.specialty: Tonkotsu ramen with a light, aromatic-oil-enriched pork-bone broth; the house 'Rakuichi-aji' (楽いち味, a lighter tonkotsu) and 'Chotteri-aji' (ちょってり味 — slightly rich) styles are the calling cards, served with a choice of thin or medium-thick noodles; gyoza and vegetable tempura round out the menu.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog reviews confirm the Nishi-ku location ~590m from Meijo-Park Station, the light aromatic tonkotsu broth, the 楽いち味 and ちょってり味 styles, thin/medium-thick noodle choice, ~10 counter seats, a solo owner, and the beer-and-appetizer izakaya feel.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No information available. Open counter kitchen in a 10-seat shop makes cross-contamination highly likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tonkotsu tare in Japanese ramen shops standardly contains wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broth and toppings are pork-based; no plant-based lane exists.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergy handling information found; the shop has no online menu disclosures and is cash-only with no reservation system, making advance allergy communication difficult.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 10-seat counter shop with a convivial but Japanese-language-only environment; the owner is friendly, but no English signage or menus are evident.

Some plain salt-grilled (shio) skewers could theoretically be lower-risk, but cross-contamination on shared grills is unaddressed. Celiac diners should call ahead and confirm soy sauce type and grill sharing practices before visiting.
nagoya_yakitori_arai.vegan_detail: A dedicated yakitori specialist built around charcoal-grilled chicken and meat skewers. No plant-based or vegan options are listed on any reviewed source. Hidden animal content (chicken fat, dashi) is likely throughout.

chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled yakitori featuring Nagoya Cochin (名古屋コーチン), a prized heritage chicken breed local to Aichi Prefecture, paired with an abundant selection of Japanese sake.

anecdotes.text: Opened 20 November 2024 in a quiet neighbourhood near Asama-cho Station, just west of Nagoya Castle. Reviewers found the quality-to-price ratio almost too generous — one calling the food 'delicious in one word, far superior to other yakitori shops' — with early praise for chicken heart (hatsu) and the springy, moist Nagoya Cochin.

Not safe for celiac or wheat allergy.
nagoya_chuka_soba_shirakabe_aoi.vegan_detail: The broth is built on animal stock — chicken carcass, pork bone, and beef — with bonito (katsuobushi) dashi also referenced by reviewers. Signature chashu pork is a standard topping. There are no plant-based options on the menu. Not suitable for vegans.

chef_bio.origin: Hida-Takayama, Gifu Prefecture (culinary inspiration); shop in Nagoya's Shirakabe neighbourhood since 1997
chef_bio.background: The shop was founded in 1997 by the Sawa family in the Shirakabe district northeast of Nagoya Castle. Ryuichiro Sawa took it over from his parents at age 35 and continues to run it today. He is also the founder of the Fujiyama 55 tsukemen chain (now 55style Co.), but this original family counter — an eight-seat, cash-only shop — is where his roots lie.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithfully carrying on the gentle, deeply savory Takayama-style ramen the shop's first generation created. Sawa preserves the inherited chuka-soba recipe while adding his own items (miso ramen, maze-soba) over the years.
chef_bio.specialty: Takayama-style shoyu ramen — a clear soy broth drawn from chicken bones, pork and beef, served with thin, house-made high-hydration wavy noodles

anecdotes.text: The shop's Takayama-style recipe traces to its first-generation founders; reviewers recount an obsession with a Hida-Takayama taste that could not be forgotten, and repeated trips to Takayama to study and perfect the style — lore reflected in the broth's distinctive sweetness and depth.

Despite a dark-coloured shoyu broth, the soup delivers a gentle, not harsh flavour — reviewers consistently note the appearance is more assertive than the taste, which is soft and umami-rich (animal stock of 鶏ガラ, トンコツ, 牛肉).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog and aunblog confirm the 1997 founding, the first-generation Takayama recipe now inherited, house-made high-hydration noodles, and the dark-but-gentle chicken/pork/beef broth; 55style/Fujiyama55 and the aunblog confirm owner 澤竜一郎 inherited the shop from his parents at 35 and founded Fujiyama 55.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat; this restaurant uses shoyu tare in its broth and no tamari or wheat-free alternative is mentioned anywhere.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broth is animal-based (chicken, pork, beef, and bonito); no plant-based cooking zone exists in this tiny 8-seat counter kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: Tiny 8-seat counter shop with no English signage or menu; ordering is straightforward but a point at the menu approach is needed for non-Japanese speakers.

nagoya_osteria_olmo.gf_detail: Italian cuisine in which pasta (wheat flour containing gluten) is central. Many wheat-using items — semolina fritto, bucatini, gnocchi and more. Use of soy sauce, dashi, etc. is unknown. Guests are advised that with notice given by two days in advance the restaurant will consider accommodating allergies, but there is no information on a dedicated gluten-free menu or cross-contamination prevention. Celiacs must confirm details directly in advance.
nagoya_osteria_olmo.vegan_detail: No fully vegan menu. Centered on Italian cuisine that makes heavy use of meat, fish and dairy (eel, guinea fowl, stracciatella cheese, etc.). It is noted that dietary requests conveyed by two days in advance may be accommodated ('dislikes/avoided ingredients up to two days ahead'). However, the extent of accommodation depends on how the course can be altered.
nagoya_osteria_olmo.hours_raw: Tue–Sat 18:00–23:00 (L.O. 21:00), closed Sun and Mon. Irregular temporary closures and occasional Sun/Mon opening (announced on Instagram).
nagoya_osteria_olmo.notes: Owner-chef Kazuya Sato trained at Aroma Fresca in Ginza and elsewhere before opening this restaurant in Nagono, Nagoya in November 2014. The space is a renovated machiya townhouse built in 1941, standing along Nagoya's 'Shikemichi,' characterized by a warm, wood-based atmosphere.

roles: オーナーシェフ（佐藤一也）
chef_bio.origin: 名古屋市西区那古野、2014年11月開業
chef_bio.background: オーナーシェフの佐藤一也氏は、銀座のアロマフレスカ（Aroma Fresca）や名古屋の個人店などで研鑽を積んだのち、東京での修業を経て名古屋に移り、2014年11月に那古野に当店を開いた。西区の「式見道（しけ道）」沿いに建つ1941年（昭和16年）築の町家を改装した空間で、当時の建具を活かした木を基調とする温かみのある雰囲気が特徴。
chef_bio.philosophy: 「日本の恵みを感じる一皿」を追求しつつ、あくまでイタリア料理の技法・エッセンスを損なわない料理づくりを信条とする。単なる「和イタリアン」に陥らない独自性を意識し、自然派ワインと合わせて提供する。
chef_bio.specialty: 日本の旬食材を用いたイタリア料理。市場の鮮魚・肉や、全国の農家から直接仕入れる自然栽培野菜を惜しみなく使い、香りと温度にこだわった一皿を提供する。

anecdotes.text: 店名「OLMO」は、店側の説明ではイタリア語で「ケヤキ（欅）」を指す言葉とされ、欅のテーブルを囲んで温かいイタリア料理と自然派ワインを楽しむという、土地に根ざした料理への意志が込められている。
ヒトサラに寄稿した推薦シェフは「カジュアルながらも非常に繊細で美味しい。関東の有名店で修業したシェフが作り出す季節ごとのメニューと、細部に至る丁寧な仕込みが随所に感じられる」と評している。

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: WEB大人の名古屋 and Gault&Millau confirm chef 佐藤一也, Nov 2014 opening, the 1941 machiya on Shikendo in Nagono, Tokyo (incl. Ginza Aroma Fresca) training, the Japanese-ingredient-forward-but-not-wa-Italian philosophy, natural wine, and the shop's stated OLMO=keyaki name-story. No published sommelier named 愛さん could be verified, so that role was removed.

gf_cross_contamination.text: 専用グルテンフリー調理器具・フライヤーの分離使用に関する情報は公式サイト・各種レビューとも一切記載なし。パスタ・セモリナ粉・小麦フリットを多用するキッチンでの交差汚染リスクは高いと考えられる。

soy_sauce_wheat.text: 醤油・だし（小麦含有の可能性）の使用有無についての情報は公開されていない。イタリア料理が主体だが、日本の旬食材を多用するため隠し味として使用している可能性を排除できない。

vegan_cross_contact.text: 乳製品（ストラッチャテッラ、ゴートチーズ等）・魚介・肉を同一キッチンで扱う。ヴィーガン専用調理ラインの情報なし。

staff_allergy_handling.text: 「アレルギーや苦手食材は2日前までにお知らせいただければ対応します」と案内されている（食べログ情報）。対応の具体的範囲（代替食材の内容・除去の確実性等）は不明。セリアックや重篤なアレルギーの方は予約時に直接詳細を確認することを強く推奨。

positives.text: 完全予約制のため、事前にアレルギー・食材の希望を伝える機会が確保されている。少人数制（15席）で、シェフが一人ひとりの状況に配慮しやすい環境。

cultural_comfort.note: 完全予約制の高級イタリアン。日本語での事前コミュニケーション（アレルギー等の申告）が必須で、英語対応の確認情報はない。

nagoya_marunouchi_soba.gf_detail: Traditional soba tsuyu is made with wheat-containing soy sauce (醤油). Tanuki soba — the signature menu item — is topped with tenkasu (tempura batter scraps), which are fried in oil shared with wheat-battered tempura. Buckwheat soba noodles can contain wheat depending on blend (no juwari/100% soba confirmed here). No GF accommodation or awareness indicated at this casual ticket-machine shop. Not appropriate for celiac diners.
nagoya_marunouchi_soba.vegan_detail: The broth is described as 和風出汁 (Japanese-style dashi), which at a standard casual soba shop of this type is virtually always made with katsuobushi (bonito flakes). No vegan-friendly broth option is indicated anywhere. Menu items include meat soba (肉そば). This place is not suitable for vegans.

nagoya_la_menkuitei.gf_detail: Standard ramen shop using wheat noodles. Soy sauce in the broth is almost certainly wheat-containing (standard Japanese shoyu). nagoya_la_menkuitei.vegan_detail: All broths are animal-based: chicken clear broth or tonkotsu (pork bone). No plant-based broth options found. Toppings include chicken chashu and pork chashu. Gyoza are also on the menu. No vegan options identified across any source reviewed.
nagoya_la_menkuitei.hours_raw: Mon–Sat 11:30–14:30, 18:00–23:00; Sun & holidays 11:30–15:00, 17:30–22:00. Closures listed as irregular on Tabelog; one source (nagoya-meshi.com) cited Wednesday closures but this may be outdated.
nagoya_la_menkuitei.notes: [Mom & Pop] La・麺喰亭 opened on June 5, 2013 in the quiet Shomokucho neighborhood of Nagoya's Higashi Ward, a short walk from Higashioote Station. It operates as a small independent counter ramen shop with approximately 20 seats.

chef_bio.background: La・麺喰亭 opened on 5 June 2013 in the quiet Shomokucho neighborhood of Nagoya's Higashi Ward, a short walk from Higashioote Station. It operates as a small independent counter ramen shop.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen favors a health-conscious, low-oil approach: reviewers consistently note you can finish the soup without heaviness. Lunch sets include complimentary rice and pickles, and affordable add-ons (chashu rice bowls, gyoza) keep the experience accessible.
chef_bio.specialty: 鶏レモンラーメン (Chicken Lemon Ramen, ¥870) — a salt-based clear broth infused with chicken umami, topped with sliced lemon, tender chicken chashu, and white scallion. The broth is intentionally low-oil, emphasizing clean chicken flavour with a bright citrus lift. A second broth option — tonkotsu (pork bone) — is available for those preferring a richer bowl.

anecdotes.text: One reviewer described the lemon ramen as 'not just novelty — it was genuinely delicious,' noting that the acidity complements rather than overwhelms the simple broth, making it ramen you'd want to eat endlessly.
The shop is described by regulars as 'a cozy place where you can chat about ramen with the friendly owner,' signaling an engaged, hands-on proprietor running a tight counter operation.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog confirms the 5 Jun 2013 opening, Shomokucho/Higashi-ku location near Higashiote, cash-only counter operation and 'friendly owner' feel; nagoya-meshi confirms the 鶏レモンラーメン at ¥870, salt-based low-oil clear chicken broth with lemon and chicken chashu, the tonkotsu alternative, and lunch rice/pickles.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese shoyu (wheat-containing soy sauce) is used in ramen broths at this type of shop; no tamari or wheat-free alternative is mentioned in any source.

cultural_comfort.note: Counter-only ramen shop with Japanese-language menus displayed above the kitchen; no English signage noted, but solo dining is common and the ordering process is straightforward point-and-pay at the counter.

nagoya_yakitori_goryo.gf_detail: No GF claims found anywhere. Standard yakitori tare (basting sauce) and shoyu-based seasonings almost certainly use wheat-containing soy sauce. The course includes a chicken dashi soup whose thickeners and seasonings are unknown. A yakitori kitchen grilling whole chickens over charcoal has no dedicated fryer risk, but cross-contact from shared utensils and sauces is a real concern. Guests with celiac disease must contact the restaurant directly before booking to ask about soy sauce type and tare ingredients.
nagoya_yakitori_goryo.vegan_detail: The entire menu is chicken-only omakase. Courses include chicken dashi soup, multiple grilled chicken cuts, and ikura (salmon roe) on the finishing rice dish. No plant-based alternatives exist and there is no indication the kitchen can accommodate vegan requests.
nagoya_yakitori_goryo.hours_raw: Mon–Sat & holidays 17:30–22:30 (food L.O. 21:30, drink L.O. 22:00), closed Sun
nagoya_yakitori_goryo.notes: [Mom & Pop] 焼鳥ごりょう opened in July 2024 in a renovated historic townhouse in Nagono (那古野), one of Nagoya's most atmospheric old districts near Shikemichi.
